title: Digital Game-Based Learning in Early Childhood: Trends, Gaps, and Future Directions
text_snippet: Digital Game-Based Learning in Early Childhood: Trends, Gaps, and Future Directions Abstract With the increasing integration of digital devices into early learning environments, digital game-based learning (DGBL) has gained growing attention as a promising pedagogical approach in early childhood education. To better understand the current landscape of DGBL in early learning, this review examined 41 recent studies conducted across diverse international contexts, focusing on study designs, game implementation, pedagogical frameworks, and reported learning outcomes. Results revealed variation in the design and delivery of DGBL interventions, yet overall positive outcomes across various learning domains. The findings also indicated the need for more theory-driven and longitudinal research, along with improved consistency in reporting practices, to strengthen the evidence base and support the effective integration of DGBL in early childhood education.

title: From Resistance to Readiness: An Ecological Governance Analysis of Digital Integration in U.S. Early Childhood Education
text_snippet: From Resistance to Readiness: An Ecological Governance Analysis of Digital Integration in U.S. Early Childhood Education Abstract The COVID-19 pandemic disrupted early childhood education across the United States, exposing longstanding inequities and accelerating the integration of digital technologies. Historically, technology in early learning contexts was approached with caution, shaped by concerns regarding screen exposure and fragmented policy guidance. This study argues that the post-pandemic era requires a transition from precautionary resistance to structurally aligned digital readiness grounded in developmental science, equity, and ethical governance. Drawing on Bronfenbrenner’s ecological systems theory and critical policy analysis, the study examines how federal legislation, state regulation, professional standards, and institutional capacity collectively shape digital technology integration in early childhood education. Through conceptual policy analysis and illustrative state contrasts, the findings reveal systemic misalignments between infrastructure expansion, professional preparation, and ethical oversight. title: Buy Smart: Introducing Responsible Consumption in Early Childhood Education: A Play-Based Didactic Sequence on Food, Waste, and Environmental Impact
text_snippet: Buy Smart: Introducing Responsible Consumption in Early Childhood Education: A Play-Based Didactic Sequence on Food, Waste, and Environmental Impact Abstract This study reports on a design-based, game-based learning (GBL) intervention aimed at fostering early understandings of responsible consumption in early childhood education. Building on a previous pilot phase in which teachers provided feedback on the Buy Smart cooperative board game, a revised version of the game was embedded within a two-session learning situation sequence designed to address food origin, transport distance, and waste generation. The intervention was implemented in a classroom of 25 five-years-old children. Data were collected through pre- and post-intervention elicitation tasks, classroom observations, children’s affective ratings, and teacher feedback, and analysed using an exploratory mixed-methods approach. The findings indicate that children’s criteria for judging which foods had the greatest environmental impact shifted from a narrow focus on visible leftovers toward a broader consideration of distance, transport, and pollution. title: The Perception of Schemas and Gender Bias in the Attribution of Distributive Actions
text_snippet: The Perception of Schemas and Gender Bias in the Attribution of Distributive Actions Abstract This study investigated the early development of gender bias in the context of distributive actions. Children aged 2.5, 3.8, 5, and 8 years were presented with events in which a hidden distributor performed fair or unfair distributions of resources, and were then asked to identify the distributor by choosing between a schematic male and a schematic female figure. Children aged 3.8 years attributed fair distributions more frequently to the male figure, while 5-year-olds attributed unfair distributions more frequently to the male figure. No significant gender-based attributions were found at 2.5 or 8 years of age. Analyses by sex of participant revealed a gender bias among male 3.8-year-olds, who attributed fair distributions preferentially to the male figure, and a gender prejudice among female 8-year-olds, who attributed fair distributions to the female figure and unfair distributions to the male figure. Taken together, these findings provide additional evidence for an early-emerging gender bias in distributive reasoning and support prior literature on the later consolidation of gender prejudice. title: StoryMat-Robot: From Activating Narrative and Transmedia Competences in Prospective Teachers to the Development of Computational Thinking
text_snippet: StoryMat-Robot: From Activating Narrative and Transmedia Competences in Prospective Teachers to the Development of Computational Thinking Abstract This study stems from the implementation of the StoryMat-Robot (SMR) project within initial teacher education for Early Childhood Education. It focuses on the design of didactic proposals supported by transmedia narratives featuring robots and materialised through floor mats, with the aim of activating teachers’ Computational Thinking (CT). The objective is to examine whether this transmedia creative process—based on adapting literary works and films—enables the development of CT dimensions alongside narrative and transmedia competences. A quantitative methodology with a descriptive and analytical approach was adopted. The SMR proposals were assessed using a set of indicators, examining narrative coherence, the logic of the route, the suitability of the challenges posed, the integration of digital resources, the use of artificial intelligence, robot functionality, and the adequacy of the mat design. title: Early Childhood Singing in Diverse Socioeconomic Backgrounds in South Africa
text_snippet: Early Childhood Singing in Diverse Socioeconomic Backgrounds in South Africa Abstract Research highlights the benefits of singing in early childhood for the development of cognitive, language, emotional and social skills. Grounded in this theoretical framework, this article draws on data from Statistics South Africa’s, The General Household Survey (2023), to examine patterns of parental singing across different socioeconomic groups. This survey does not measure the efficacy of singing in early childhood, but it does provide insights into disparities in the exposure to home singing among young children. Various analytical techniques were used to analyze the data, such as descriptive analysis, bivariate analysis, regression analysis, and multivariate analysis. The findings of the analyses highlight the disparities in music exposure and singing practices across socioeconomic backgrounds and educational levels in South Africa. Children from high socio-economic backgrounds have access to regular singing activities in the home as well as access to better early childhood development programmes that incorporate regular singing activities. The findings underscore the need for policy intervention and structured programmes that promote access to singing opportunities

title: Maternal Responsiveness and Young Children’s Inhibitory Control in the Ecuadorian Amazon
text_snippet: Maternal Responsiveness and Young Children’s Inhibitory Control in the Ecuadorian Amazon Abstract Executive functions, including inhibitory control, develop rapidly in early childhood and are critical for academic, social, and emotional adaptation. Maternal responsiveness—timely, appropriate, and supportive reactions to a child’s needs—has been shown to foster executive function (EF) in Western, Educated, Industrialized, Rich, and Democratic (WEIRD) populations, yet evidence is scarce in low-resource, Indigenous settings. The present longitudinal study examined the influence of early maternal behaviors observed in toddlerhood on later inhibitory control at school entry among Indigenous children living in the Ecuadorian Amazon. Fifty mother–child dyads from two rural Amazonian communities were assessed when the children were about 26 months old (T1) and again about 30 months later (T2). Maternal behaviors including responsiveness, encouragement and teaching were observed and coded from a 10 min free-play session, child cognitive ability was assessed, and mothers completed a parenting stress questionnaire at T1. title: From Practice to Policy: Developing Quality Criteria for Multilingual Education in Early Childhood Settings
text_snippet: From Practice to Policy: Developing Quality Criteria for Multilingual Education in Early Childhood Settings Abstract Early multilingual education is increasingly recognised as central to equity, inclusion and children’s linguistic rights in Early Childhood Education. However, policy aspirations are often weakly connected to everyday classroom practices, and there is still limited guidance on what constitutes quality plurilingual pedagogy in early childhood settings. This study addresses this gap by developing and validating a context-sensitive framework of quality criteria for multilingual Early Childhood Education. A modified Delphi method was used within a sequential mixed-methods design. In an initial qualitative phase, expert reflections on real-world plurilingual practices were analysed using grounded theory procedures, resulting in the formulation of six criteria. These criteria were subsequently validated through a quantitative round with 29 experts from 11 countries. title: Early Childhood Educators’ Doings to Facilitate Children’s Participation in Play: A Scoping Review and Thematic Analysis of Research Literature
text_snippet: Early Childhood Educators’ Doings to Facilitate Children’s Participation in Play: A Scoping Review and Thematic Analysis of Research Literature Abstract The United Nations’ fourth Sustainable Development Goal emphasises quality education for all, including early childhood education. In early childhood education and care (ECEC) quality largely hinges on inclusive access to play for all children, which is contingent on educators’ practices. Recognising the critical role of educators’ actions, this article provides a scoping overview of existing knowledge on specific practices, conceptualised as “doings,” that educators do to facilitate children’s engagement in play. The concept of “doings”, drawn from the theory of practice architecture, encapsulates the diverse “modes of action” through which educators can support play. By reviewing and thematically analysing ten years of empirical studies (from 2012 to 2021) we identify different play facilitating practices educators utilise and by that contributes to the academic discourse on practice-developing research.

title: Navigating Uncertainty: Early Childhood Educators’ Interpretations of Echolalia in Practice
text_snippet: Navigating Uncertainty: Early Childhood Educators’ Interpretations of Echolalia in Practice Abstract This qualitative study explores the experiences of early childhood educators and teachers as they encounter echolalia in professional practice. Echolalia, commonly defined as the repetition of heard language, appears in both typical language development and as a feature of neurodevelopmental difference. While previous research has explored echolalia through clinical or parental lenses, there is limited insight into how it is experienced by professionals in early childhood settings. Semi-structured interviews were conducted with 63 early childhood professionals working across Australia. Data analysis occurred through a reflexive thematic approach, with three overarching themes identified. First, professionals reported difficulty in discerning whether a child’s repeated language was a typical stage of language development or an indicator of echolalia. Second, regardless of its nature, professionals responded to all language, interaction, and communicative attempts. Third, participants expressed concern about misidentifying echolalia. title: Enhancing Early Childhood Education for Sustainability: Integrating (Re) Connect with Nature into the 7R Themes
text_snippet: Enhancing Early Childhood Education for Sustainability: Integrating (Re) Connect with Nature into the 7R Themes Abstract This study aims to examine how forest school practices support Early Childhood Education for Sustainability (ECEfS) and to explore how sustained engagement with nature extends or challenges the existing 7R themes (Reduce, Reuse, Recycle, Redistribute, Respect, Reflect, and Rethink). Using a qualitative case study design, the research was conducted in a forest school in Türkiye and involved semi-structured interviews with five preschool teachers, as well as structured and unstructured classroom observations. Data were analysed through a systematic three-level content analysis guided by the 7Rs. The findings reveal that ECEfS is enacted through interconnected practices of reducing consumption, reusing materials, recycling through composting, redistributing resources, rethinking, reflecting, and fostering respect. However, sustained and immersive engagement with nature emerged as a distinct pedagogical dimension not fully captured by the existing 7Rs, leading to the identification of an eighth theme: Reconnect with Nature. title: Stability and Change in Social-Emotional Profiles of Head Start Children: A Latent Transition Approach
text_snippet: Stability and Change in Social-Emotional Profiles of Head Start Children: A Latent Transition Approach Abstract This study examined the diverse social-emotional development of a population-based cohort of 1,921 Head Start children, focusing on the variability in developmental patterns over time. We used data from the 2014 Family and Childhood Experiences Survey to conduct a latent profile analysis of teacher-rated social-emotional competencies, including children’s approaches to learning, classroom social cooperation, and behaviors such as aggression, hyperactivity, and anxiety/withdrawal. We identified four social-emotional profiles (i.e., Adaptive, Average, Moderate Risk, and High Risk) at two points (fall 2014 and spring 2015). Further, latent transition analysis revealed both stability and change within these profiles over time, with significant demographic differences in profile transitions. While some children in the Moderate Risk and High Risk profiles demonstrated persistent challenges, others showed improvement by transitioning to lower-risk profiles. title: Father–Child Shared Reading Behaviours and Emergent Literacy: Insights from the Daddy Book Club
text_snippet: Father–Child Shared Reading Behaviours and Emergent Literacy: Insights from the Daddy Book Club Abstract This study investigates the relationship between children’s emergent literacy, fathers’ involvement in early literacy development, and shared book-reading activities within early childhood education (ECE) settings. Using an experimental pre-test/post-test design, it evaluates the effectiveness of the Daddy Book Club , an emergent literacy intervention aimed at enhancing fathers’ reading behaviours to support their children’s literacy development. Data were collected using the Parent–Child Reading Behaviour Checklist (Collings in N Z J Speech Lang Ther 67:22–30, 2012) and the Preschool Word and Print Awareness Assessment (PWPA) (Justice in Child Lang Teach Ther 17:207–225, 2001). Findings indicate that the intervention improved fathers’ engagement in shared reading, leading to increased print-referencing behaviours and enhanced vocabulary and print awareness in children. These results underscore the importance of fathers as active participants in early literacy development and offer valuable insights for future research and educational practices aimed at strengthening parental involvement in children’s literacy learning within ECE settings.

title: Beyond Visible Compliance: A Case Study of a Young Child’s Transition to Nursery Care
text_snippet: Beyond Visible Compliance: A Case Study of a Young Child’s Transition to Nursery Care Abstract Early transition to nursery care is often understood through visible protest at separation, yet some children show distress in quieter ways. This qualitative single-case study examined the first nursery transition of Elif, a 3-year-old girl in Türkiye with no reported developmental diagnosis who was experiencing regular separation from her parents for the first time. The dataset comprised 22 Tavistock-informed observation protocols gathered across arrival and departure moments over 3 months, eight seminar protocols, and semi-structured interviews with Elif’s mother, father, and teacher. Analysis combined chronological reconstruction, focused coding of interview transcripts, and cross-source triangulation. Findings indicated a marked contrast between outward composure and inner strain. Although Elif often appeared calm at drop-off, classroom observations showed silent crying, bodily tension, hesitant communication, reduced appetite, and continued reliance on a stuffed rabbit interpreted as serving a transitional function. title: Discrepancies in Assessing Preschool Readiness: A Comparative Study of Parent and Teacher Perspectives on Three-to-Four-Year-Olds
text_snippet: Discrepancies in Assessing Preschool Readiness: A Comparative Study of Parent and Teacher Perspectives on Three-to-Four-Year-Olds Abstract This study investigates preschool readiness in children aged 3–4 years through a comparative analysis of parent and teacher assessments. While early childhood development is a critical predictor of future academic success, there remains a significant research gap regarding how different informants perceive developmental milestones during the initial transition to preschool. Using the Preschool Education Questionnaire, data were collected from a large sample of parents and teachers in the Czech Republic to evaluate cognitive, motor, social, and language domains. The findings reveal systematic differences between informant groups, particularly in language and social-emotional ratings, where parents tended to provide more optimistic evaluations than teachers. These results highlight the necessity of multi-informant assessment frameworks to obtain a holistic view of a child’s development. By identifying these perceptual discrepancies, the study contributes to a more nuanced understanding of school readiness and offers practical implications for early intervention and parent-teacher communication in preschool education.
